findings: The preserved source asks for Median of Two Sorted Arrays / LeetCode 4 and identifies binary search, but it does not preserve a Java API, null behavior, both-empty behavior or a runtime sortedness-validation requirement.
The candidate keeps those missing interface details explicitly answer-side instead of presenting them as recovered source constraints.

The partition invariant is correct: the left-side cardinality is fixed first, j is derived from i, and because each input is internally sorted the only cross-boundary violations are Aleft > Bright or Bleft > Aright.

The binary-search direction is coherent and monotone: Aleft > Bright moves i left, while Bleft > Aright moves i right; searching only the shorter array keeps the derived partition within the other array bounds.

Odd and even totals are handled from the same partition; logical infinities cover endpoint cuts, duplicate values are accepted with <= comparisons, and long boundary arithmetic prevents int overflow in the even median average.

The standalone Java implementation matches an independent direct-merge oracle across fixed boundaries and 5000 deterministic generated sorted-array pairs, including empty-side, duplicate and Integer.MIN/MAX cases.

The answer does not fabricate production data sizes or latency experience; it explicitly bounds the O(log(min(m,n))) claim to O(1) random access arrays and notes that untrusted-input sortedness validation changes the complexity.
